content: Baking powder is a dry chemical leavening agent commonly used in cooking, particularly in baking. Traditional baking powder consisted of a mixture of tartaric acid and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), often with a small amount of flour added to moderate its strength. When dissolved in water, the acid and bicarbonate react to release carbon dioxide gas, which expands and forms bubbles, thereby leavening the mixture. Modern baking powders are typically double-acting, meaning they contain two types of acid salts. One reacts at room temperature, causing an initial rise as soon as the dough or batter is mixed, while the other reacts at higher temperatures during baking, resulting in further leavening. Baking powders that contain only low-temperature acid salts are referred to as single-acting. Many recipes involve a technique called creaming, where butter and sugar are beaten together to introduce tiny air bubbles, which the leavening gas will expand further. Common low-temperature acid salts include cream of tartar, calcium phosphate, and citrate. High-temperature acid salts are often aluminum-based, such as calcium aluminum phosphate. These aluminum salts are not only found in many baking powders but also in non-dairy coffee creamers. Excessive dietary aluminum may pose health risks, and aluminum-free baking powders are available for individuals concerned about aluminum intake or sensitive to its taste. However, many commercial products, such as muffin mixes and bakery goods, still contain aluminum-based leavening agents. While various forms of baking powder were available in the early 19th century, modern versions were developed by Alfred Bird. Eben Norton Horsford, a student of Justus von Liebig, began studying baking powder in 1856 and eventually created a variety named after Count Rumford. German pharmacist August Oetker popularized baking powder by marketing his mixture to housewives. The recipe he developed in 1891 is still sold in Germany under the name Backin. Oetker began mass production of baking powder in 1898 and patented his technique in 1903. The development of Rumford Baking Powder was recognized in 2006 as an ACS National Historical Chemical Landmark for its role in making baking easier, faster, and more reliable. Baking powder is most commonly used in quick breads such as pancakes, waffles, and muffins. Typically, one teaspoon (5 mL) of baking powder is used to leaven a mixture containing one cup (200–250 mL) of flour, one cup of liquid, and one egg. However, if the mixture is acidic, the additional acids in the baking powder may remain unreacted, imparting an unpleasant chemical taste to the food. Ingredients like buttermilk, lemon, yogurt, citrus, or honey can increase acidity. In such cases, some of the baking powder is replaced with baking soda. For example, a recipe with one cup of flour, one egg, and one cup of buttermilk requires only ½ teaspoon of baking powder, with the remaining leavening provided by the reaction between buttermilk acids and ¼ teaspoon of baking soda. Baking powder can be substituted in recipes by combining baking soda with an acid. A common recommendation is to mix two parts cream of tartar with one part baking soda. Vinegar, particularly white vinegar, is another common acidifier in baking. For instance, some traditional chocolate cake recipes call for a tablespoon or two of vinegar. When recipes already include acidic ingredients like buttermilk or yogurt, baking soda can be used without cream of tartar or with a reduced amount. Alternatively, lemon juice can replace some of the liquid in the recipe to provide the necessary acidity to activate the baking soda. During World War II, Byron H. Smith, an inventor from Bangor, Maine, created a substitute product called Bakewell for American housewives who could not obtain baking powder, cream of tartar, or baking soda due to wartime shortages. Bakewell, a mixture of sodium pyrophosphate and cornstarch, remains part of regional culinary history. When combined with baking soda, it functions as a single-acting baking powder, with sodium pyrophosphate serving as the acid. The use of aluminum compounds as food additives has raised concerns due to scientific evidence regarding the safety of aluminum in the diet. Elevated levels of aluminum have been found in the brain tissue of individuals with neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease. While the use of aluminum cookware has declined due to these concerns, aluminum continues to enter the diet through baking powder, aluminum cookie sheets, and other sources.
